section_summary: This section covers State Department records from February 1932 to July 1939 regarding religious affairs, institutions, and state religious policies in Japan and its empire under decimal file 894.404. Key matters include official debates over whether Shrine Shinto constitutes a religion, the rise of popular sects like Tenrikyo, Catholic diplomatic relations following the 1937 Tokyo visit of Cardinal Dougherty, and Japanese political overtures toward the Islamic world, including the opening of Tokyo's first mosque. The section culminates with the enactment and detailed translation of the Religious Organizations Law of 1939, which centralized state control and supervision over Buddhist, Shinto, and Christian bodies under the Ministry of Education while extending tax privileges to recognized religious organizations.

subfiles.about: Letter recommending Christian businessman M. Hirayama and his film project on Japanese Christian martyrs to President Hoover.
subfiles.summary: George McCune of Union Christian College introduces Christian businessman M. Hirayama to President Hoover, who made the film "The Twenty Six Martyrs of Japan" and wants an audience about a sound version in Los Angeles.
subfiles.title: Letter from George Shannon McCune to President Herbert Hoover regarding M. Hirayama and Film on Christian Martyrs

subfiles.about: Instruction regarding protocol for requesting a Presidential audience for visiting film producer M. Hirayama.
subfiles.summary: Bundy instructs Seoul Consul General Davis to tell McCune a presidential audience can't come by personal letter, only by a formal request from the applicant's diplomatic representative in Washington.
subfiles.title: Instruction to American Consul General at Seoul regarding Request for Presidential Audience for M. Hirayama

subfiles.about: Document file note and excerpt from Tokyo despatch regarding the governmental commission studying whether Shrine Shinto is a religion.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 62: a 1929 Home Ministry commission of Shinto scholars and officials couldn't agree whether Shrine Shinto is a religion and suspended work; if so, students couldn't be compelled to visit shrines to war dead.
subfiles.title: Document File Note and Despatch Extract regarding Shrine Shinto Commission

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting press clippings on the Tenrikyo sect and its autumn festival at Tambaichi.
subfiles.summary: Consul Richard F. Boyce transmits clippings from The Japan Advertiser and The Japan Times & Mail regarding the Tenrikyo religion and the dedication of its massive new headquarters sanctuary at Tambaichi, Nara Prefecture. The reports describe the history and teachings of foundress Miki Nakayama, comparing her to Mary Baker Eddy, and detail ceremonies led by Kwancho Masayoshi Nakayama around the sacred Kanrodai monument. Tenrikyo claimed six million adherents and drew hundreds of thousands of pilgrims to the festival, reflecting a broad popular religious revival in Japan.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 19 from Yokohama regarding Tenrikyo Sect with Newspaper Clippings

subfiles.about: Inquiry regarding a presidential or secretarial message of greeting to the General Conference of the Methodist Church in Japan.
keywords: General Conference of the Methodist Church in Japan
subfiles.summary: William Quillian, a fraternal delegate to the Methodist Church in Japan's General Conference, asks Hull or Roosevelt for a brief greeting, to be used only to foster friendship.
subfiles.title: Letter from William F. Quillian to Secretary of State Cordell Hull requesting Message of Greeting to Methodist General Conference in Japan

subfiles.about: Refusal of request for official government message of greeting to a non-governmental church conference in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull, proud of American missionaries' work in Japan, declines to send a greeting, since diplomatic custom bars officials from official greetings to nongovernmental conferences abroad, or to recommend that Roosevelt do so.
subfiles.title: Letter from Secretary of State Cordell Hull to William F. Quillian declining to issue Message to Church Conference in Japan

subfiles.about: Document file note and excerpt from Tehran despatch concerning Japanese overtures toward Islam and diplomatic conversions.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 486 from Tehran quotes an article on Japan's interest in Islam, including Muslim students, a Japanese Quran and alleged diplomatic conversions; Hornibrook thinks the Kabul minister's conversion was political or oil-motivated.
subfiles.title: Document File Note and Despatch Extract regarding Moslems in Japan and Diplomatic Converts to Islam

subfiles.about: File note and excerpt on a Damascus Masonic group planning to send an Islamic missionary scholar to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Beirut report: a Damascus Masonic group, Al-Ahrar al-Masuni, designated an Islamic scholar to preach Islam in Japan and planned a fundraising drive for a second.
subfiles.title: Document File Note and Report Extract regarding Damascus Masonic Group Sending Moslem Missionary to Japan

subfiles.about: Detailed reporting on the visit to Japan of Cardinal Dougherty, his imperial audience, and his bowing at the Meiji Shrine.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports extensively on the February 1937 Tokyo visit of Cardinal Dennis Dougherty, Archbishop of Philadelphia, returning from the International Eucharistic Congress in Manila as Papal Legate. Grew describes diplomatic arrangements for separate imperial audiences for Cardinal Dougherty and Apostolic Delegate Paolo Marella, a formal dinner hosted by Premier and Foreign Minister Senjuro Hayashi, and an Embassy luncheon. Notably, Cardinal Dougherty paid homage and bowed at the Meiji Shrine, an act that deeply impressed Japanese authorities and publicly affirmed the Vatican's October 1936 decree permitting Catholics to attend civil Shinto ceremonies.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2276 regarding Visit to Japan of Cardinal Dougherty, Archbishop of Philadelphia

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for a paper on Christian education and church-state relations in Japan transmitted by A. L. Warnshuis.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: A. L. Warnshuis sends an American missionary's 1936 paper on Christianity and the state in Japan, on government restrictions and Christian education.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Observations concerning Christianity and the State in Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet regarding inquiries directed to Christian organizations in Japan concerning their views.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Osaka Consul Makinson's Despatch 12 on Japanese authorities requiring Christian bodies to give written statements of their views.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Christian Organizations Asked for Statements on Christianity

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing Tokyo Despatch No. 3036 on the political motives behind Japan's embrace of Islam.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury summarizes Despatch 3036 on the Tokyo Mosque dedication: rumors Italy funded Arab visitors, the Turkish Ambassador boycotted, and he agrees Japan's courting of Muslims is political, not religious.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum regarding Tokyo Despatch No. 3036 on Japan and Mohammedans

subfiles.about: Comprehensive report on the dedication of Tokyo's first mosque, international Muslim visitors, and Japan's Islamic policy.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the May 12, 1938 dedication of Tokyo's first mosque, with Prince Hussein of Yemen and Saudi Minister Wahba, links it to Hirota's view of Islam as a bulwark against communism, notes the Turkish Ambassador's refusal to attend, and Pan-Islamic leagues.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3036 regarding Japan and Mohammedans

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for an article transmitted by H. Parker Dunlop discussing missionary work and the military situation.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: H. Parker Dunlop's article on religion in the Japanese Empire, on missionary achievements and the Sino-Japanese conflict's damage to missions.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Article on Religion in the Japanese Empire

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 3722 on proposed religious control legislation.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs summarizes Despatch 3722 on the Religious Organizations Bill in the Diet, giving legal definitions and regulation; the Embassy expects no unreasonable interference with Christian missions for now.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum regarding Proposed Legislation on Religious Organizations

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the introduction and key terms of the Religious Organizations Bill in the Japanese Diet.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the Religious Organizations Bill centralizing supervision in the Education Ministry, classing recognized bodies in five categories with Christianity equal to Shinto and Buddhism and tax exemptions; mosques were excluded, but it isn't aimed at American missions.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3722 regarding Proposed Legislation for Definition of the Status of Religious Organizations and for the Control Thereof

subfiles.about: Protest and constitutional documents from an American Muslim group denouncing Japanese discrimination against Islam.
subfiles.summary: L. Selim-Glick of the proposed American Islamic Mosque Association in Los Angeles protests the Diet's exclusion of Islam from recognized religions, declares March 25 a day of mourning, and encloses a constitution and Pan-Islamic Congress correspondence.
subfiles.title: Letter and Resolution from American Islamic Mosque Association Protesting Japanese Diet Discrimination Against Islam

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 3910 and its translation of the Religious Organization Law.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury summarizes Despatch 3910 with the Religious Organization Law translation: Dooman says missionaries and Japanese Christians accept it calmly, welcoming tax exemptions and clear administrative authority despite onerous regulations.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum regarding Transmission of Religious Organization Law

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting an English translation of the enacted Religious Organization Law (Law No. 77 of 1939).
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires a.i. Eugene H. Dooman transmits a complete translation of the Religious Organization Law (Law No. 77), passed by the Diet and promulgated on April 8, 1939, with an Imperial sanction signed by Premier Hiranuma, Education Minister Araki, Home Minister Kido, and Finance Minister Ishiwata. The despatch outlines the statute's centralization of administrative authority under the Ministry of Education, procedures for juridical incorporation, tax exemptions, and government powers to suspend or dissolve groups that disturb public peace or contravene imperial subjects' duties. Dooman reports that Christian bodies expect no insurmountable difficulties under the new regime.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3910 Transmitting Translation of the Religious Organization Law (Law No. 77 of 1939)

subfiles.about: Military intelligence report analyzing the legal provisions and religious effects of the Religious Organizations Law.
subfiles.summary: G-2 Report 9819 reviews the Religious Organizations Law: Christianity is recognized beside Shinto and Buddhism, it distinguishes organizations from lesser societies, and lists recognition requirements and tax exemptions.
subfiles.title: G-2 Intelligence Report No. 9819 regarding the Religious Organizations Law
subfiles.to: War Department G-2 / Department of State

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet regarding letters documenting the persecution of Christian workers in China.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Consul Smyth's Despatch 2151 enclosing missionary H. W. Hubbard's and the Nanking consul's accounts of persecution of Christian workers.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Persecution of Christian Workers
